odeComponent.htmlView:
Hello! Welcome to this exciting journey through the history of music. Throughout the course, we’ll be setting various exams to test your level of musical analysis, taking into account stylistic features, historical context and the connection between past eras and the present day.

To make sure you’re prepared, copy the following musical analysis template into your Music Passport. You’ll be able to use it in the exam.

MUSICAL PASSPORT
MUSICAL ANALYSIS TEMPLATE

1. TECHNICAL AND SONIC ANALYSIS
1.1. Instrumentation:

  • Voices only (A cappella): Male / Female / Mixed / Choir?
  • Instruments only: Main instrument family / Soloist / Orchestra / Synthesized?
  • Mixed: Voices + Instruments.

1.2. Predominant Texture:

  • Monophony / Monophonic: A single melodic line (in unison or octaves).
  • Polyphony / Polyphonic: Multiple independent melodies moving simultaneously or in imitation (counterpoint).
  • Homophony / Homophonic: Multiple parts moving together in block chords with the same rhythm.
  • Melody and Accompaniment: A clear solo lead melody supported by an underlying chordal/instrumental accompaniment.

1.3. Rhythm and Tempo:

  • Free rhythm: No steady beat or meter (flexible, tied to breath or speech).
  • Strict / Measured rhythm: Clear, steady beat with an identifiable meter (duple / triple).
  • General Tempo: Slow (Lento) / Moderate (Moderato) / Fast (Allegro).
  • Tempo changes: Steady pulse / Accelerando / Ritardando.

1.4. Form / Basic Structure:

Organization:

  • Continuous (Through-composed): Follows the text without clear repeated sections.
  • Binary (AA or AB) / Ternary (ABA).
  • Rondo / Refrain (A - B - A - C - A -...).
  • Theme and Variations.
  • Popular Song Form: Intro / Verse / Chorus / Bridge / Solo / Build-Up / Drop / Outro / Coda.

Interaction:

Direct: The whole ensemble or soloist performs continuously from start to finish.
Alternating / Dialogue: Soloist vs. ensemble (Call and response / Responsorial) or two groups alternating.


2. CONTEXT, FUNCTION, AND LANGUAGE
2.1. Original Social Function:

  • Religious / Liturgical: Worship, prayer, church/temple service.
  • Courtly / Aristocratic: Palace dancing, private chamber music, display of status and power.
  • Popular / Secular Entertainment: Traditional folk dance, protest song, public celebration, commercial theatre, concert hall.

2.2. Text and Language:

  • Instrumental (no lyrics).
  • Vocal with text: Latin / Vernacular language (Spanish, French, English, Italian...)?

2.3. Connection to its Era:

Explain in 1–2 sentences what this music reflects about its historical period and why it sounds that way.(e.g., the importance of religion in the medieval era, Renaissance humanism, Baroque theatrical drama, Enlightenment order and balance, Hippie movement, British Punk movement...).

odeComponent.htmlView:
The Middle Ages span a long period of time (5th to 15th centuries).  The main characteristics of this period were:

  • Society was divided into closed groups with virtually no social mobility: the nobility and the clergy (the privileged classes) and the peasantry (who worked the land).
  • The political and economic system was feudalism:  based on a relationship of vassalage, whereby the king or the nobles granted land in exchange for loyalty and military protection.
  • The Catholic faith dominated everyday life: the power of the Church dominated daily life, culture and thought of the era.

During this period, musical forms such as Gregorian chant and secular music predominated, and it was during this time that polyphony first emerged.


What are we going to learn?

1. Medieval music

    1.1 – Monophonic religious music: Gregorian chant.

    1.2 – Monophonic secular music: troubadours and trouvères.

    1.3 – The Cantigas of Alfonso X the Wise.

    1.4 – The birth of polyphony.

    1.5 - Instruments of the Middle Ages.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Throughout the first few units, we’ll hear a lot about texture and types of texture. Let’s find out what they mean.

Texture: this is the way in which different melodies, rhythms and voices are combined and relate to one another within a musical work.

Tipos de textura:

  • Monophony (or monody): This consists of a single melodic line without any accompaniment or harmony. If several people sing or play exactly the same notes at the same time, this is also monophony.
  • Homophony: Several voices or melodies sound at the same time with different notes, but sharing the same rhythm (they move together, forming blocks of chords).
  • Polyphony: Several voices or melodic lines sound at the same time, but are independent of one another and follow different rhythms. The melodies intertwine and compete for prominence.
  • Melody and accompaniment: a melody stands out against an accompaniment.

odeComponent.htmlView: When we talk about medieval music, one might think that music was only performed in churches, but this is not the case. Secular music developed mainly thanks to the troubadours and trouvères in the 12th and 13th centuries, particularly in France. The troubadours and trouvères were noble and educated people. They composed both the lyrics (poetry) and the music for their songs, although these were usually performed by minstrels or bards.

1.3. Cantigas de Alfonso X el Sabio
1.3. Cantigas by Alfonso X el Sabio

odePagStructure.blockName: Cantigas by Alfonso X el Sabio

odeComponent.htmlView:
One of the great treasures of Spanish medieval secular music is the huge collection of Cantigas de Santa María, by Alfonso X el Sabio (1221–1284). We know that the King was not only the person who organised this collection, he also participated in it, composing some of the cantigas . This collection features almost 2,000 miniatures, providing very valuable information about everyday life, the blend of cultures in Spain and the study of instruments of the time.

Cantiga refers to a type of poetic-musical composition in the Galician-Portuguese language. Note: although the lyrics deal with religious themes, it is considered secular music.


Thanks to the surviving miniatures we have invaluable information about the instruments of the period and evidence that they were played whilst the songs were being sung.

Cantigas recounted the miracles of the Virgin (some were in praise of these). Cantigas are structured by continuously alternating between the chorus and different verses. At the end of each verse, the last lines use the same rhyme and music as the chorus. One of the most famous cantigas is Cantiga de Santa María n.º 100, known as «Santa María, strela do dia».

odeComponent.htmlView:
As we have explained previously, monophony was the predominant musical texture. However, just as architecture evolved from the Romanesque to the Gothic style, music moved from monophony to polyphony.
Capilla románica de La Soledad, Palazuelos (Guadalajara). Catedral gótica de Santa María, Burgos.



Polyphony is a musical texture that involves composing music for several voices that sound simultaneously.


We can divide medieval polyphonic music into two periods:

1. Ars Antiqua: The earliest religious polyphony (9th to 13th centuries)

The earliest polyphonic works did not emerge until the 9th century, and they developed from Gregorian chant. Taking Gregorian melodies as their basis, other voices were added at intervals of a fourth or a fifth, since, according to medieval thinking, these were the intervals that sounded harmonious. These early polyphonic works were known as organum.

In the 12th and 13th centuries, an important musical school developed around Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris. Léonin and Perotin stood out as composers of polyphony within this school. These composers developed a variant of the organum known as melismatic organum.

During the 13th century, new and more complex types of polyphonic composition emerged, such as the conductus and the motet.

  • The conductus is a polyphonic composition based on newly created melodies (rather than Gregorian chants, as in the organum).
  • Motets (mot means ‘word’ in French) emerged as compositions for several voices. In the earliest medieval motets, each voice had its own text, sometimes in different languages.

2. The Ars Nova: secular polyphony (14th century)

In the 14th century, polyphony continued to develop through composers such as Philippe de Vitry and Guillaume de Machaut. Secular music began to take on greater importance, and secular polyphonic genres, such as the chanson, emerged.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Monophonic music

  • Religious: Gregorian chant (Latin, monophonic, a cappella, anonymous, religious and free-rhythm).
  • Secular: troubadours and trouvères (solo singing, vernacular languages, varied themes (love, war…), accompanied by instruments, composers with signed works).

The ‘Cantigas’ of Alfonso X the Wise:

  • Written in Galician-Portuguese. Although they refer to the Virgin Mary, they are considered secular music.

Polyphony

  • Ars Antiqua
    • Organum: adding further lines to an existing Gregorian chant.
    • Conductus: the same concept as the Organum but based on newly composed melodies.
    • Motets: compositions for several voices.
  • Ars Nova
    • Greater emphasis on secular music.
    • Chanson: a secular polyphonic genre.
